fields.Headline: China factory output contracts as demand weakens in July
fields.Body:
China's factory activity shrank in July as demand faltered, according to the latest official purchasing managers' index (PMI) released on August 1, fueling concerns that the world's second-largest economy is losing momentum. The reading, which fell below the 50-point threshold separating growth from contraction, underscores persistent weaknesses in both domestic and external orders, despite a string of policy measures aimed at bolstering growth.

The downturn is broad-based, with smaller manufacturers hit hardest. Sub-indices for new orders and output both weakened, while employment continued to shed jobs. The data comes as Beijing balances support for manufacturing against longer-term structural shifts, including overcapacity in some industries and sluggish property investment, which remains a drag on industrial demand.

For foreign investors, the weak PMI adds to a cautious outlook for China's industrial sector. It may also revive speculation over fresh stimulus, though policymakers have emphasized patience, preferring targeted rather than broad-based measures. Exporters face mixed signals: while global demand for electronics and green-energy goods has been resilient, softness in consumer goods and machinery orders suggests a fragile recovery.

With officials signaling that they will monitor the situation closely, the next several months will be pivotal. If the contraction deepens, pressure will mount on Beijing to act more decisively, potentially through infrastructure spending or further monetary easing. For now, the data point to a manufacturing sector treading water, a reality that global supply-chain planners must factor into their China strategies.
fields.Why It Matters: For investors and brand leaders, a contracting factory PMI signals weaker demand for components, machinery, and consumer goods, likely squeezing margins and inventories. It sharpens the case for China-specific risk hedging and underscores the importance of watching for fresh stimulus, which could revive industrial spending in the second half.
fields.Author: ChinaPulse Editorial
fields.Summary: China's manufacturing activity fell into contraction in July, the latest sign that domestic demand is faltering, stoking concerns about the pace of economic recovery. The official PMI came in below the 50-mark, missing expectations.

fields.Headline: China's 'Three New' economy adds 1.2 trillion yuan in value in 2025
fields.Body:
China's National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) released data on the value added of the 'Three New' economy for 2025, measuring industries and business models built on new technologies, new industries, and new business formats. The report, published on July 31, provides a granular look at a segment Beijing views as key to lifting productivity and achieving 'high-quality' growth.

While the overall value added remains a fraction of the country's $18 trillion GDP, its growth rate has consistently outpaced the broader economy since the NBS began tracking it in 2016. The 'Three New' umbrella spans everything from green-energy manufacturing and e-commerce platforms to cloud computing and smart logistics, capturing both established tech giants and a proliferating cohort of startups.

The data matter beyond the raw numbers. They signal where policy support and capital are flowing. Central planners are channeling subsidies, tax breaks, and procurement preferences into these sectors, in effect creating a subsidized orbit of innovation. For multinational companies, the implication is double-edged: competition from Chinese 'Three New' firms is intensifying, yet so are opportunities for suppliers of components, software, and services that feed into these ecosystems.

Critically, the 'Three New' economy is also a barometer of China's decoupling of statistical reporting from traditional industrial structures. As Beijing rewires measurement, foreign analysts will increasingly need to parse these new categories to understand where growth is actually being produced—and where the risks lie.
fields.Why It Matters: For investors, the 'Three New' data map which sectors will receive sustained policy tailwinds, from advanced manufacturing to digital services. Brand leaders should align China strategies with these prioritized industries—positioning themselves as partners to a state intent on building self-reliant tech and green supply chains.
fields.Author: ChinaPulse Editorial
fields.Summary: China's statistics bureau revealed that the 'Three New' economy—new industries, new business models, and new technologies—contributed approximately 1.2 trillion yuan to GDP in 2025, underscoring its growing role in the country's growth strategy.

fields.Headline: China's short-drama boom hits regulatory reality
fields.Body:
China's short-drama industry is about to hit a regulatory wall. On July 31, the National Radio and Television Administration (NRTA) released the 'Micro-Drama Development and Management Measures' (Order No. 16), a 54-article rule taking effect September 1. It's the sector's first dedicated regulatory framework, elevating oversight from scattered notices to a structured legal code.

The key change is a risk-tiered system based on investment scale and subject matter. Productions with large budgets or that touch politically sensitive themes—including politics, military affairs, religion, or national security—must apply for filing approval before shooting and pass content review before release, obtaining a 'Micro-Drama Distribution License' printed by the NRTA. The review process takes up to 20 working days and includes expert panels. Smaller, non-sensitive projects face a simpler process, with approval authority delegated to provincial regulators.

For an industry that exploded on platforms like Douyin and Kuaishou, with daily revenue potential in the tens of millions, compliance now shapes the path to market. Smaller studios without resources may find themselves squeezed out, while established players with legal teams gain a moat. The rule also introduces content standards: promoting traditional culture, avoiding vulgarity, and preventing unauthorized adaptation of foreign works.

In effect, short dramas are transitioning from a wild-west of user-generated creativity to an administered content category. The shift mirrors the trajectory of online video in China—first chaotic, then regulated—and signals that as the format matures, so too will official oversight, influencing everything from production timelines to creative boundaries.
fields.Why It Matters: For global brands eyeing short-drama marketing, the new rules mean tougher compliance, longer lead times, and the need to work with licensed producers. It also consolidates market share among top-tier creators, making them the safer partners for sponsored content in a regulatory tightening environment.
fields.Author: ChinaPulse Editorial
fields.Summary: China's National Radio and Television Administration has issued its first formal regulation for short-form web dramas, effective September 1, reclassifying them as licensed content. The 54-article rule builds on earlier patchwork guidelines, aiming to professionalize a booming but often chaotic sector.

fields.Headline: Brunello Cucinelli lifts outlook on China-led strength
fields.Body:
Brunello Cucinelli, the Italian luxury fashion house known for its understated cashmere, has raised its 2026 revenue guidance after reporting first-half sales growth of 9.5%, led by robust performance in China. The company now projects annual growth of 10-11% at constant exchange rates, up from the 10% it had previously guided. The results, released on July 31, surprised some analysts who had been braced for a slowdown in global luxury demand.

China's contribution was particularly notable, according to the company, as high-net-worth consumers continue to splurge on exclusive, quiet-luxury labels. The brand's positioning around artisanal craftsmanship and 'humanistic' values appears to resonate with Chinese buyers seeking distinctiveness amid a sea of logo-driven fashion. Growth was also broad-based across regions, with Europe and the Americas holding up, but the Asian momentum was the standout.

The upgraded guidance suggests luxury spending in China remains resilient despite broader economic uncertainty. It also reflects a wider trend: high-end brands with a strong local following are weathering the downturn better than mass-market players. For competitors, this signals that focusing on exclusivity and brand story can pay off, but also that overexposure to a single market is a double-edged sword—should Chinese demand soften, luxury houses must be nimble.

For investors, the earnings beat and guidance raise reinforce that positioning matters more than sector averages in the current environment. Brunello Cucinelli's stable of wealthy, loyal customers, particularly in Asia, provides a buffer that many mid-tier brands lack.
fields.Why It Matters: For luxury and premium brands, the Chinese consumer remains a powerful growth engine even as the economic cycle turns. Brunello Cucinelli's results are a template: cultivate a curated identity, invest in heritage, and tap into affluent Asian buyers. It also warns that reliance on China demands both brand resilience and adaptability.
fields.Author: ChinaPulse Editorial
fields.Summary: Italian luxury house Brunello Cucinelli reported a 9.5% rise in first-half revenue, driven by robust demand in China, prompting an upgrade to its full-year sales forecast. The brand now expects growth of 10-11% at constant exchange rates, up from a previous 10%.

fields.Headline: Malaysia targets China's lower-tier cities to boost tourism
fields.Body:
Malaysia is stepping up its efforts to lure travelers from China's booming second- and third-tier cities, according to industry sources. The country's tourism board is reportedly preparing a campaign to promote the Southeast Asian destination beyond the traditional hubs of Beijing, Shanghai, and Guangzhou, recognizing that consumption power is increasingly evident in inland provincial centers.

The shift aligns with a broader trend of Chinese tourism spreading outward from the top-tier cities. Residents of cities like Chengdu, Hangzhou, or Wuhan are now taking more international trips, and Malaysia—with its mix of cultures and relatively accessible visa policies—stands to benefit. The planned push includes working with local tour operators, travel platforms, and possibly influencers who have outsized reach in these markets.

For the travel industry, the implications are clear: competition for the Chinese tourist is intensifying, and destinations must tailor offerings to a more diverse demographic. Malaysia's move also reflects a learning curve—while its tourism numbers have recovered, the profile of the visitor is changing, with a greater share of middle-class families seeking leisure and cultural experiences rather than just shopping.

For airlines and hospitality groups, this strategic pivot could drive new flight routes and hotel development in second-tier Chinese cities. It also suggests that other destinations will need to recalibrate their marketing, focusing on digital channels and partnerships that resonate with consumers beyond the major coastal markets.
fields.Why It Matters: Tourism boards and travel brands should observe Malaysia's pivot as a case study in adapting to China's changing outbound market. Brands in retail, F&B, and entertainment could capitalize on the influx of Chinese travelers by developing tailored offerings that appeal to consumers from lower-tier cities, who often exhibit distinct spending patterns compared to first-tier counterparts.
fields.Author: ChinaPulse Editorial
fields.Summary: Malaysia is intensifying its tourism push into China's second- and third-tier cities, seeking to diversify beyond the major metros. The strategy aims to tap rising travel demand from inland regions, a move expected to benefit airlines, hotels, and travel agencies.

fields.Headline: Chinese PE Fund CPE Acquires Swiss Outdoor Brand Mammut
fields.Body:
Chinese private equity firm CPE Yuanfeng has agreed to acquire Mammut, the Swiss manufacturer of premium outdoor apparel and equipment, according to Luxe.CO. The deal adds a storied European brand to the portfolio of a Chinese investor known for targeting consumer and technology assets.

Mammut, which has operated for more than 160 years, is considered a benchmark manufacturer in the global outdoor sector, known for its technical climbing gear and high-performance jackets. The acquisition underscores the growing appetite of Chinese capital for established Western brands with strong heritage and premium positioning.

For global brand owners, the deal highlights how Chinese investors are not only seeking growth-stage assets but also mature icons with untapped potential in the Asia-Pacific region. With China's outdoor recreation market expanding rapidly, the new ownership could accelerate Mammut's retail expansion and digital transformation in the world's second-largest economy.

The transaction may also face regulatory scrutiny in Europe, given the strategic importance of heritage brands. However, if completed, it would mark one of the largest recent outbound deals in the sporting goods sector, signaling continued Chinese interest in acquiring valuable intellectual property and brand equity abroad.
fields.Why It Matters: This acquisition gives a Chinese PE firm direct control over a leading European outdoor brand, potentially reshaping its distribution and marketing strategy in Asia. Global investors should watch how CPE leverages Mammut's heritage to capture China's booming outdoor and lifestyle segments.
fields.Author: ChinaPulse Editorial
fields.Summary: CPE Yuanfeng has acquired Swiss outdoor gear maker Mammut, marking a major cross-border deal that gives Chinese capital a stake in a 160-year-old European heritage brand.

fields.Headline: China's Domestic Flight Bookings Jump 62% for First August Weekend
fields.Body:
Flight bookings for the first weekend of August have surged 62% compared with the previous week, according to data from Chinese travel platform Qunar, as reported by Pinchain. The spike reflects the height of the summer holiday season, with families and young travelers taking advantage of school breaks.

The strong booking figures come amid a broader recovery in China's travel industry, which has seen pent-up demand release after years of pandemic disruptions. Domestic routes to popular destinations like Sanya, Chengdu, and Xi'an are reportedly seeing high load factors, pushing up ticket prices.

For airlines and hospitality groups, the trend signals sustained consumer spending on experiences, even as broader economic growth moderates. The data also suggests that Chinese travelers are prioritizing domestic getaways over outbound trips, partly due to lingering visa frictions and currency considerations.

Looking ahead, industry analysts expect the momentum to continue through late August, with bookings for the upcoming mid-autumn festival also showing early strength. The overall picture is one of cautious optimism for China's travel value chain, from carriers to hotels and online travel agencies.
fields.Why It Matters: The 62% jump in weekend bookings indicates robust domestic travel demand that could lift airline and hotel revenues in Q3. Brand owners in tourism-related sectors should adjust inventory and marketing to capture this peak season.
fields.Author: ChinaPulse Editorial
fields.Summary: Qunar data shows weekend flight bookings up 62% as summer travel demand peaks, signaling a robust rebound for China's domestic tourism sector.

fields.Headline: Tuniu Projects Fresh Passenger Traffic Peak in Mid-August
fields.Body:
Tuniu, a Chinese online travel agency, anticipates a new round of travel peak in mid-to-early August, according to Pinchain. The forecast is based on booking patterns and search volume data from its platform, which shows a surge in last-minute holiday bookings.

This expected peak follows an already busy July, with many Chinese families taking advantage of school holidays. The mid-August wave is likely driven by families who delayed their vacations to avoid the initial rush, as well as younger travelers seeking short breaks before the new semester begins.

Destinations popular for cooler climates, such as Yunnan, Guizhou, and Inner Mongolia, are expected to see particularly high demand. Tuniu also notes that package tours and customized trips are gaining traction, reflecting a shift toward higher-value travel products.

The sustained travel demand bodes well for the broader services sector, as consumer spending remains resilient despite economic headwinds. However, businesses should be prepared for potential price competition and capacity constraints as the season reaches its peak.
fields.Why It Matters: A second August peak means travel demand is stronger than initially projected, offering opportunities for secondary destinations and niche tourism products. Investors in travel and leisure should monitor whether this momentum carries into the autumn season.
fields.Author: ChinaPulse Editorial
fields.Summary: Chinese online travel agency Tuniu expects another wave of travelers in mid-August, extending the summer boom as vacationers return from earlier trips.

fields.Headline: China's Visa-Free Policy Fuels Travel Rebound With Canada
fields.Body:
China's expanded visa-free policy is driving a resurgence in two-way travel between Canada and China, according to a report from CGTN. The policy, which allows citizens from select countries to enter China without a visa for short stays, was extended to include Canadian passport holders in a bid to stimulate tourism and business exchanges.

Data cited by CGTN indicate a marked increase in flight bookings and search queries from Canadian travelers to Chinese cities like Beijing, Shanghai, and Xi'an. Chinese airlines have responded by adding capacity on key routes, while Canadian carriers are also eyeing expansions.

The visa-free arrangement is part of a broader Chinese push to revive inbound tourism and restore international connectivity after years of pandemic isolation. For Canada, the policy lowers barriers for business travelers and tourists, potentially fostering closer economic ties.

However, travel volumes remain below pre-pandemic levels, and factors such as airfare costs and geopolitical tensions could temper growth. Nonetheless, the policy is a positive step toward normalizing cross-border movement, with ripple effects for airlines, hotels, and travel agencies in both countries.
fields.Why It Matters: The visa-free policy significantly reduces friction for Canadian travelers, opening new opportunities for tourism operators and companies with cross-border business interests. Brands targeting Chinese consumers should also note the potential for increased Canadian visitor spending.
fields.Author: ChinaPulse Editorial
fields.Summary: China's visa-free entry policy has boosted travel between Canada and China, with flight bookings and tourism interest rising notably, according to CGTN.

fields.Headline: Deepexi's AI Revenue Surges 209% as Losses Narrow Sharply
fields.Body:
Deepexi, a Chinese enterprise AI solutions provider, posted a 115% year-on-year revenue increase to 284 million yuan ($39 million) in the first half of 2026, according to its first interim report as a listed company, as reported by 36Kr. The company turned profitable in the second quarter, with net profit of about 30 million yuan, and cut its first-half net loss by 89.6% to 32 million yuan.

The core growth driver was DeepexiOS, the company's AI-level enterprise operating system platform, which generated 226 million yuan in revenue, up 209.2% year-on-year. This segment now accounts for 79.6% of total revenue, up from 55.3% a year earlier, as the company pivots away from its legacy data intelligence business.

Gross margin improved to 56.5%, up 1.5 percentage points, with DeepexiOS achieving a 57.2% margin, up 2 points. The earnings improvement reflects both scale economies and a richer product mix, with AI software replacing lower-margin services.

The results are the latest evidence of accelerating AI adoption among Chinese enterprises, as companies seek to modernize operations with on-premise and platform-based solutions. Deepexi's performance suggests that demand for practical AI applications remains strong, even as investors question the sustainability of pure-play AI valuations.
fields.Why It Matters: Deepexi's strong AI-driven growth and path to profitability offer a bellwether for the Chinese enterprise AI sector. Companies evaluating AI vendors should note the shift toward platform-based offerings, which may consolidate market share among leaders like Deepexi.
fields.Author: ChinaPulse Editorial
fields.Summary: Chinese enterprise AI firm Deepexi reported a 115% revenue jump and a first profitable quarter, driven by its AI operating system platform, signaling strong corporate adoption.
